exhibits.title: The Clock That Sets the Budget
exhibits.text:
The glass at the centre of this hall empties every twenty milliseconds and turns itself over. That is 50 Hz, and it is not a metaphor for anything. It is the control rate a manipulation policy has to hold. Robots need 30 to 50 Hz. Whatever the policy does, it must finish inside that window, every window, forever.

This single constraint decided which generative method won for robot control. It is a LATENCY argument, not an expressiveness argument.

A diffusion policy is expressive enough. It handles multimodal action distributions, it emits continuous values, and it works. But it needs roughly 100 denoising steps per chunk, and 100 forward passes cannot fit in 20 milliseconds. The method is not wrong; it is late.

Flow matching produces a usable chunk in about 10 steps, because the path it integrates is straight and the velocity along it is close to constant. π0 uses exactly 10. Two steps already give something usable. That is the entire reason a technique developed for image generation ended up on robot arms.

Three more things follow from the clock and are laid out around this hall: which alternatives it eliminates, the caching trick that makes even 10 passes affordable, and an experiment on a deliberately ambiguous task that shows what the fast alternative, plain regression, silently gets wrong.

exhibits.title: Four Candidates, Three Requirements
exhibits.text:
An action head must satisfy three things at once. It must preserve MULTIMODALITY, when several behaviours are valid, it must be able to produce one of them rather than their average. It must be CONTINUOUS, since precision in a joint command is precision in the grasp. And it must be FAST enough for a 20-millisecond window.

  discrete tokens   multimodal ✓   binning loses precision   autoregressive decode slow
  MLP regression    collapses ✗    continuous ✓              fast ✓
  diffusion head    multimodal ✓   continuous ✓              ~100 steps ✗
  flow matching     multimodal ✓   continuous ✓              ~10 steps ✓

Each of the first three fails a different requirement, and each failure is structural rather than a matter of tuning. Binning is a quantisation of the output space. Regression to a single point is what a squared-error objective on a deterministic function means. A hundred denoising steps is what a curved probability path costs.

Flow matching is the only row with three ticks, and it earns the third by integrating a straight path. Not by being a better generative model than diffusion: by being a cheaper one to sample.

exhibits.title: The Cache That Buys the Hertz
exhibits.text:
Ten passes over a 3.3B model would still miss the budget. They are not what happens.

The observation does not change during integration. Image tokens and text tokens do not depend on τ at all. The scene is the same scene at τ=0 and at τ=0.9. So their keys and values are computed ONCE and cached across all ten integration steps. Only the action-side tokens, roughly 51 of them (the state token and the 50-step chunk), re-run each pass.

  cost = one 3B forward pass + ten 300M forward passes
  NOT  = ten 3.3B forward passes

This is the KV cache from the Library of Keys, applied along an unusual axis. There, keys and values were cached across positions in an autoregressive decode. Here they are cached across NOISE LEVELS in an integration loop. Same mechanism, same justification: if a computation does not depend on the loop variable, hoist it out of the loop.

The general form of the rule appears in the gotcha lists as compute the conditioning ONCE, outside the integration loop. Ignore it and you recompute a 3B backbone ten times per control step, which is the most common way to build a policy that is correct and unusably slow.

exhibits.title: The Experiment That Settles It
exhibits.text:
A deliberately bimodal task, built to expose the one failure that does not show up in the loss.

The setup: identical observation every time, and a demonstrator who sometimes reaches LEFT around an obstacle and sometimes reaches RIGHT. Both are correct. Nothing in the input distinguishes them. Target action magnitude 1.0.

Flow matching, trained on those demonstrations, split roughly 45/55 between left and right. It SAMPLES A MODE AND COMMITS, draws a noise vector, integrates, and arrives at one valid behaviour or the other.

An MLP regression baseline, trained on the same data, produced 0.418, a path straight down the middle, into the obstacle. That is not a bug in the baseline. It is what minimising squared error against an ambiguous target REQUIRES: the conditional mean of the two modes, which is the average of going left and going right, which is going nowhere useful.

The damning part is that its action-MSE looked perfectly healthy throughout. The failure is invisible in the training curve and obvious the moment the arm moves.

exhibits.title: The Bench Book
exhibits.text:
The numbers from the bimodal run, and what each of them is evidence for.

I. THE MEASUREMENT. Target action magnitude 1.0. A policy that commits to one mode should land near 1.0; a policy that averages the modes lands near the middle, well short.

  flow matching,  1 step   → |x_end| 0.243    too coarse
  flow matching,  2 steps  → |x_end| 0.833    already usable
  flow matching,  5 steps  → |x_end| 0.964
  flow matching, 10 steps  → |x_end| 0.988    diminishing returns
  flow matching, 50 steps  → |x_end| 0.998
  regression               → |x_end| 0.418    ← COLLAPSED to the middle

II. READING THE STEP COUNT. The column climbs fast and then flattens. One step is a single Euler jump across the whole path and is genuinely too coarse. Two steps already reach 0.833. By ten the answer is 0.988 and the remaining forty steps buy 0.010. This is the empirical justification for π0's choice of 10: it sits exactly at the knee, where more integration stops being worth its latency.

III. READING THE REGRESSION ROW. 0.418 is not undertrained. It is the correct minimiser of the objective it was given. With one observation mapping to two valid actions, squared error is minimised by the conditional MEAN, and the mean of left and right is straight ahead, into the obstacle the demonstrator was avoiding. The model learned the task perfectly and the task, as posed to a regressor, was wrong.

IV. WHY THE LOSS DID NOT WARN ANYONE. Its action-MSE looked healthy the whole way. Averaging is exactly what the metric rewards. Any evaluation that scores a policy by its distance to demonstrated actions will rate a mode-collapsed policy well, because the mean is close to everything and correct about nothing. Multimodal tasks need multimodal evaluation: look at the distribution of rollouts, not the mean error.

V. WHY FLOW MATCHING ESCAPES IT. The flow head is not a function from observation to action. It is a function from (observation, noise, τ) to a velocity. Different noise draws follow different trajectories and land on different modes, 45% left, 55% right in this run. The stochasticity that makes it generative is what lets it commit.

VI. THE COROLLARY FOR REAL ROBOTS. Manipulation demonstrations are multimodal almost by default. Which side to approach from, which grasp to use, whether to reposition before lifting, human demonstrators are not consistent, and the inconsistency is not noise to be averaged away. Every mode a regressor blends is a behaviour it can no longer produce.

exhibits.title: The Portrait of the Bench Engineer
exhibits.subtitle: on trusting the wrong number
exhibits.text:
"The loss curve was fine. That is what I want you to sit with for a moment. It came down, it flattened where I expected it to flatten, and every number on my dashboard said the policy had learned the task.

"Then I ran it, and the arm went straight into the obstacle. Every time. Not erratically, confidently, reproducibly, into the obstacle.

"It had learned the average of two correct answers, and I had built a metric that thinks the average of two correct answers is a good answer. Squared error against a demonstration set will always say that. The middle is close to everything.

"So: judge these policies by what they DO. Roll them out and look at the distribution. If your demonstrators disagreed with each other, a healthy policy should disagree with itself in the same proportions, mine splits about forty-five to fifty-five, and that is the number I now check first. Action-MSE tells you how close you are to the mean of the data. It does not tell you whether the mean is a place you want the arm to go."

exhibits.title: Commit, or Average Into the Wall
exhibits.caption: The deliberately bimodal experiment. (a) One observation with two valid answers: the demonstrator sometimes goes LEFT and sometimes RIGHT around the obstacle. The sampled flow-matching paths pick a side and commit, roughly 45/55 between them. The grey line is what a regression head answers, the MEAN of the two modes, which drives straight into the obstacle. (b) The measured end-magnitude against a target of 1.0: flow matching reaches 0.243 at one step, 0.833 at two, 0.964 at five, 0.988 at ten and 0.998 at fifty, while regression sits at 0.418, collapsed to the middle. The regression head's action-MSE looked perfectly healthy the whole time, which is exactly why the metric to trust is a rollout, not a loss.

exhibits.title: Why Flow Matching Won for Control
exhibits.spec:
graph TD
  C["control budget: 30 to 50 Hz, about 20 ms per decision"] --> A["discrete tokens: autoregressive decode, too slow"]
  C --> B["MLP regression: fast, but regresses to the conditional mean"]
  C --> D["diffusion head: about 100 steps, misses the budget"]
  C --> E["flow matching: about 10 steps on a straight path"]
  B --> BM["bimodal test: 0.418, collapsed into the obstacle"]
  E --> EM["bimodal test: 0.988 at 10 steps, splits 45/55 left and right"]
  E --> K["KV cache: image and text keys/values do not depend on τ"]
  K --> COST["cost = one 3B pass + ten 300M passes"]
  COST --> HZ["50 Hz achieved"]
exhibits.caption: The control budget eliminates three of four candidates. Discrete tokens decode too slowly, diffusion needs about 100 steps, and regression is fast but returns the conditional mean: 0.418 on the bimodal test, a path into the obstacle. Flow matching integrates a straight path in about 10 steps and splits 45/55 between the two valid modes. Caching the observation's keys and values across integration steps turns ten 3.3B passes into one 3B pass plus ten 300M passes, which is what actually fits in 20 milliseconds.
